911.quote_or_event: “Listen, madman: you have been trapped by false love, which is transitory, like the fading color of the safflower.”
911.explanation: Guru Arjan warns the mind that the love it has fallen into is false, bright for a moment like safflower dye and then gone. In Gurbani the safflower stands for any attachment that looks like love but cannot last.
911.tie_back: Like the Kural’s mercenary sweet words, this love is real only in appearance, and the one who trusts it is left with grief.
911.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 777, Raag Soohee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
911._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB/SikhiToTheMax (Sant Singh Khalsa); the false-love theme fits, but Guru Arjan means love of Maya in general, not a woman’s love bought with money.

912.quote_or_event: “Bronze is bright and shiny, but when it is rubbed, its blackness appears.”
912.explanation: This shabad opens with the image of polished bronze that leaves black marks when rubbed: a fine surface hiding a dark interior. According to the Janamsakhi tradition Guru Nanak sang it to Sajjan, a man who kept a pious-looking rest-house for travellers and robbed them, and who repented on hearing it.
912.tie_back: The Kural tells the wise to weigh the character behind sweet talk of virtue, and Guru Nanak’s bronze shows exactly what such testing reveals.
912.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
912._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB/SikhiToTheMax; a strong match on outward virtue over inner calculation, though the hymn is about hypocrisy in general, and the Sajjan setting is Janamsakhi hagiography.

913.quote_or_event: “Beholding an illusion, you are deceived, and on your bed, you enjoy a false lover.”
913.explanation: Guru Arjan pictures the deluded soul as a bride taken in by a mirage, lying on her bed with a lover who is not real. The false lover is Maya: an embrace that gives nothing true back.
913.tie_back: The Kural’s stranger’s corpse in a dark room and Guru Arjan’s false lover on the bed both describe an embrace with no living love in it.
913.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 460, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
913._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB/SikhiToTheMax; the empty-embrace image is close, but Gurbani’s false lover is a metaphor for Maya, spiritual rather than literal.

914.quote_or_event: “The Sovereign Lord is the nine treasures for me.”
914.explanation: Kabir says that the Lord alone is his whole wealth, while the possessions and spouse people cling to belong to God and go with no one at death. Real riches, for Kabir, are the divine treasure, not what the senses chase.
914.tie_back: As the Kural’s wise seek the wealth of grace and ignore cheap charms, Kabir counts the Lord as his true treasure and lets lesser attractions go.
914.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1158, Raag Bhairao, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
914._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB/SikhiToTheMax; matches the Kural’s contrast of true and base wealth, but the shabad does not speak of women or of paid favours.

915.quote_or_event: “You gaze upon the wives of others, O my soul; you steal and commit evil deeds.”
915.explanation: Guru Nanak speaks to his own soul and lists its faults: a wandering eye for other men’s wives, theft and wrongdoing. Self-examination of this kind, done with the Guru’s understanding, is how Sikhism expects a person to check desire before it acts.
915.tie_back: The Kural says a mind perfected by good sense will not seek low pleasures, and Guru Nanak shows that understanding at work by naming the craving and rebuking it.
915.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 155, Raag Gauree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
915._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB/SikhiToTheMax; concerns other men’s wives rather than women whose favours are for sale, so this is a next-best thematic match.

916.quote_or_event: “The Sikh ought to treat beautiful women of others as his mothers, sisters, and daughters.”
916.explanation: In a pauri describing the Gursikh’s daily conduct, Bhai Gurdas sets the standard for how a Sikh looks at women who are not his wife: as mother, sister or daughter. This became a widely cited rule of Sikh sexual ethics.
916.tie_back: The Kural says those who guard their good name will not seek the arms of women offering cheap favours, and Bhai Gurdas gives the Sikh form of that same self-respecting restraint.
916.source: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 29, Pauri 11 (English translation as published on BaniDB/SikhiToTheMax and searchgurbani.com)
916._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB; Bhai Gurdas is authoritative early exegesis, not scripture, and he gives a positive rule of conduct rather than the Kural’s argument from reputation.

917.quote_or_event: “The Dark Age of Kali Yuga is the vessel, filled with the wine of sexual desire; the mind is the drunkard.”
917.explanation: In a salok addressed to Mardana, Guru Nanak pictures sexual desire as wine and the unruly mind as the one who keeps drinking it. The cure he offers is to make truth, good deeds and modesty the mind’s real food and drink.
917.tie_back: The Kural says only a heart without self-mastery seeks arms that belong elsewhere, and this salok locates the problem in a mind that cannot stop drinking desire.
917.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 553, Raag Bihaagraa, Bihaagre ki Vaar, Salok (Mardana 1), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
917._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on srigranth.org; a good fit for the uncontrolled mind, though it speaks of kaam in general, not of hired or divided affection.

918.quote_or_event: “The mad-man’s mind is enticed by Maya, the enticer; he has taken the intoxicating drug of falsehood.”
918.explanation: Guru Arjan calls Maya mohani, the enchantress who bewitches the mind until it acts as though drugged. The word is the same one the Tamil commentators reach for when they gloss the Kural’s anangu as Mohini’s spell.
918.tie_back: The Kural compares the deceitful embrace to seizure by an enchanting spirit, and Guru Arjan’s enchantress Maya, who leaves the mind drugged and foolish, is a close Sikh counterpart.
918.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1213, Raag Saarang, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
918._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB/SikhiToTheMax; the bewitching-enchantress image is very close, but Gurbani’s Mohini is Maya itself, not a particular woman.

919.quote_or_event: “Those fools, who drink in the wine of evil-mindedness, become the husbands of prostitutes.”
919.explanation: Guru Arjan says that people who drink the wine of bad counsel become fools in the company of prostitutes. Elsewhere Gurbani holds out the hope that even the prostitute Ganika was saved by remembering the Name, so no one is beyond grace.
919.tie_back: The Kural calls such company a hell-like mire for base, undiscerning men, and Guru Arjan likewise names the evil-minded fool as the one who sinks into it.
919.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 399, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
919._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB/SikhiToTheMax; close on base men and prostitutes, but the wine is metaphorical (durmat), and Sikhism adds hope of redemption that the Kural does not.

920.quote_or_event: “The drunkards gamble and look at the wives of others.”
920.explanation: Bhai Gurdas puts drink, gambling and lust for other men’s wives in one line as a single cluster of sins, before saying that even these are less grave than turning one’s back on the Guru. The same three ruinous habits recur together in Sikh moral teaching.
920.tie_back: This is the Kural’s own triad, double-minded women, liquor and dice, named together as the companions of the ruined.
920.source: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 34, Pauri 16 (English translation as published on BaniDB/SikhiToTheMax and searchgurbani.com)
920._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB, with the pauri’s heading confirmed on searchgurbani.com; a near one-to-one triad, though Bhai Gurdas’s point is that apostasy is worse still, and his work is exegesis, not scripture.
